claims.text: Conventional W–Cu composites have suboptimal W/Cu interfaces that limit thermal transport.
Conventional W–Cu composites provide reasonable mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
A graded infiltration process can create a porous, interlinked tungsten scaffold containing a coherent, continuous high-purity copper network.
The resulting microstructure will have minimized interfacial defects and optimized W/Cu phase connectivity.
Fusion-reactor components experience high temperatures, high heat fluxes, and intense neutron irradiation.
Tungsten is relevant to fusion applications because of properties including high melting temperature, low sputtering or erosion, and low neutron activation.
Tungsten provides the mechanical durability and irradiation resistance of the proposed W–Cu composite.
Copper provides superior thermal conductivity for heat-sink service.
A coherent copper channel integrated with a tungsten skeleton reduces interfacial thermal resistance.
Conventional W–Cu composites lacking an engineered interpenetrating network have higher interfacial scattering and less efficient heat conduction.
The graded, infiltrated W–Cu composite will have higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable conventional W–Cu composite.
The graded, infiltrated W–Cu composite will preserve mechanical durability under fusion-reactor conditions.
The graded, infiltrated W–Cu composite will preserve irradiation resistance under fusion-reactor conditions.
The predicted benefits depend on precise optimization of pore size, infiltration temperature, and infiltration time.
Departures from the optimized infiltration process may eliminate thermal benefits or compromise composite integrity.
